catalog_quote: For this, we rely almost entirely on Nivens (2017), a database of over 900 Proto-Aru reconstructions with supporting reflexes. All data and Proto-Aru reconstructions in this chapter are from this database with some differences in the analysis of the Proto-Aru phoneme inventory. ... Transcriptions of data are adapted to IPA standards, with the following exceptions. The letter ‹y› is used for the palatal glide [j], Tarangan mid-close [e] and [o] are transcribed ‹ê› and ‹ô› (mid-open [ɛ] and [ɔ] are transcribed ‹ɛ› and ‹ɔ›), and unexpected stress is marked by an acute accent. (The normal pattern is penultimate stress, or final stress if the final syllable contains a mid-vowel.) The symbol ‹ʍ› represents a voiceless labio-velar fricative.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand only. The comparative database from which every published Koba form comes (Nivens 2017, as reproduced by Grimes & Edwards 2026) assumes a default of penultimate stress, or final stress when the final syllable has a mid vowel, for all Aru languages including Koba, and marks deviations with an acute. Koba forms so marked include final-stressed maŋár 'sky', ɸiɸíŋ, ekatú, kalaʍár and penult-marked wúney, oéni, maníʍey, ɸúsa, yáʍa, sírey, ʍéla, -ʍáŋar; the acute on several of the penult forms (ɸúsa, yáʍa, ʍéla) is not 'unexpected' under the stated default, so the marking is not fully consistent with the convention. No source describes Koba stress in its own right; the closest first-hand description is Hughes 2000 on Dobel (majority penultimate, c. 20% contrastive final stress, final /e o/ attract stress, final /tu ʔu/ extrametrical), a related but distinct language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Koba (Hughes 2000: 134 mentions Dobel secondary stress two syllables before the primary in the context of /a/ allophony).
new_statements.exceptions: Acute-marked Koba forms (deviations from the database default): maŋár (T6.1 p.275), (wúney) (T6.8 p.281), oéni, maníʍey (T6.11 p.284), ɸúsa, ɸiɸíŋ (T6.12 p.285), yáʍa, ekatú (T6.13 p.286), sírey (T6.14 p.287), ʍéla, -ʍáŋar (T6.15 p.288), kalaʍár (appendix).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated lexical items in comparative tables (citation forms from a wordlist-based database); no statement on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog koba1240 / ISO kpd = the three Koba villages (Koba Dangar on Baun I; Koba Seltimur and Koba Selfara on Fukarel I; pop. c. 600-870). Hughes 1987 (NUSA 27: 98-99) treated the Kobadangar data point as a dialect of Dobel (dobe1238) at 78-86% lexical similarity while noting the people consider it a separate language; Hughes 2000: 131-132 and Grimes & Edwards 2026 (Dobel-Koba subgroup, p. 288-289) treat Koba as a separate language closest to Dobel; Badan Bahasa's Peta Bahasa and Erniati et al. 2022 instead list 'dialek Koba' (Kobasel Timur, Kobasel Fara) as a dialect of Barakai (bara1367). The only first-hand stress description in the vicinity, Hughes 2000 sec. 2.4 (pp. 135-136), is of Dobel (Northern dialect, Koijabi village), not Koba.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work (Collins 1982) was marked silent and it was read in full: nothing missed there. In Schapper & Zobel 2024 (marked not-about-this-language) the reader cited only sec. 35.2.4; a second stress passage exists at sec. 35.3.3.1, p. 576 (PDF 10): 'The languages of Aru form a major exception; the base for reduplication is the stressed syllable, but stress can be initial or final' (West Tarangan, Dobel, Batuley examples). It supports the same Aru-group picture (stress lexically initial or final) and does not name Koba, so it changes nothing for the catalog record.
